A missile fired from land can be spotted. The site is fixed, satellites watch it, and the launch gives off heat and warning. A missile fired from a submarine is a different problem entirely. The boat hides under the ocean, moves where it wants, and can surface anywhere to launch with little warning. On October 14, North Korea showed it can do exactly that.

North Korean state media reported on October 15 that the country had test-fired two submarine-launched cruise missiles off its eastern coast the day before. North Korea calls them "strategic" missiles, its term for systems designed to carry a nuclear warhead. It did not name the missiles or say how far they flew, and leader Kim Jong Un is reported to have overseen the launches.

South Korea's military filled in some of the detail. Its Joint Chiefs of Staff said one missile was fired from a vertical launch tube and the other from a torpedo tube, two different ways of launching from a sub. Just as notably, South Korea said it had tracked the missiles from before they left the water all the way through the end of their flight, a quiet signal that it had been watching the submarine the whole time. U.S. Forces Korea did not immediately comment, and North Korea claimed the test had no adverse impact on its neighbors.

Why does a submarine launch matter so much? Because it is survivable. Land sites can be found and targeted first; a submarine hidden at sea is the piece that can still strike back, which is exactly why the world's major nuclear powers put missiles on subs. This was North Korea's first publicly reported submarine-launched cruise missile test since January 2024, and it fits a wider push by Pyongyang to field nuclear-armed submarines, a capability that would make its arsenal far harder to neutralize.

The stakes land squarely on the United States and its allies. Roughly 28,500 American troops are stationed in South Korea, with more in Japan, all within reach of a mobile launch platform that can hide in the ocean. It came during a busy stretch for Pyongyang, which also fired ballistic missiles earlier in October. The reassuring part, if there is one, is in South Korea's wording: it said it saw the whole thing. A hidden submarine is a serious problem, but the allies made a point of showing they were not caught blind.

For decades the American way of war was built around a small number of very expensive machines: a few exquisite jets, a few high-end systems, each one a masterpiece and each one irreplaceable if it was lost. The Pentagon just signaled that era is ending, and the number it put on the table is staggering.

Speaking at the Association of the United States Army's annual meeting in Washington on October 14, 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the Pentagon is seeking roughly 50 billion dollars, as a one-time investment, to mass-produce drones and other autonomous systems. The goal he laid out is a change in scale that's hard to picture: taking the U.S. stockpile of autonomous systems from thousands of units to millions.

Hegseth said the department expects to handle "hundreds of thousands of one-way attack systems this year and into the millions in years to come." To get there, he argued the military has to stop thinking only in terms of a few costly platforms and start buying cheap systems it can build at enormous scale, the kind of math that has reshaped the battlefield in recent conflicts, where swarms of inexpensive drones have gone up against billion-dollar equipment.

Just as important as the money is who gets to build it. Hegseth pushed to open the door to new, smaller companies in a market long dominated by a handful of giant traditional contractors, while still valuing those established firms. He also called for cutting the red tape that slows production down, telling his officials bluntly, "I want you to tell me which rules can be signed away."

This isn't starting from zero. Late last year the Army kicked off its own one-billion-dollar "Drone Dominance" effort to buy around 340,000 small drones for combat units over two years, with tens of thousands expected to reach soldiers in 2026 and hundreds of thousands by 2027. The 50-billion-dollar request still has to clear Congress, so none of it is guaranteed. But the direction is unmistakable: the most powerful military on earth has decided its next edge isn't one perfect machine, it's a million cheap ones.

Think about this for a second. The newest B-52 in the Air Force was built in 1962. The oldest crews flying it today weren't born yet when it was already old. And the Air Force has no plans to retire it, in fact, it intends to keep the B-52 in the air into the 2050s. By then the plane will have served for roughly 100 years.

The B-52 Stratofortress first flew in 1952 and entered service in 1955. Boeing built the last one, an H model, in 1962, and the H is the only version still flying today, about 76 of them. Every single one is older than the parents of the young airmen who fly them. No other combat aircraft in history has come close to that kind of run.

So why does it refuse to die? Because nothing has ever matched what it does for the price. The B-52 can haul an enormous load over intercontinental distances, carry almost every weapon in the inventory, and do it cheaply compared to newer jets. Rather than replace it, the Air Force is rebuilding it: new Rolls-Royce F130 engines to replace the originals, a modern radar, and upgraded electronics. The rebuilt aircraft gets a new name, the B-52J, and a new lease on life that stretches for decades.

That endurance has created something you almost never see in aviation. Take the family of Col. Don Sprague, who flew every B-52 model from the A all the way to the H and commanded the 23rd Bomb Squadron at Minot Air Force Base in the early 1970s. Decades later his grandson, Capt. Daniel Welch, became a B-52 aircraft commander in that very same squadron, with Daniel's father having flown the B-52 in between. Three generations of one family, all on the same plane.

And here's the part that stops people cold: because the B-52 is on track to fly for a full century, a pilot climbing into one today could be strapping into the exact same airframe his grandfather flew, and someday his own grandson might fly it too. There is no other machine of war on earth you can say that about. The B-52 was built to outlast the Cold War. It ended up outlasting almost everyone who ever doubted it, and it still has decades left to go.

The U.S. Army just gave the public its first look at what the Abrams tank is going to become, and it works very differently from the tank that has rolled into battle for the last 45 years. One of the first surprises: the driver steers it with a gaming controller.

In January 2026, the Army put the first prototype of its next-generation Abrams, the M1E3, on display at the Detroit Auto Show. It's an early demonstrator rather than a finished tank, but it previews the ideas the Army wants in the Abrams of the 2040s.

The biggest change is up top. For the first time, the Abrams moves to an unmanned turret, with no crew riding inside it. An autoloader is planned to handle the 120mm main gun, which drops the crew from four to three, all of them seated down in the hull where they're better protected. The tank is lighter than today's Abrams, and while this prototype keeps the classic turbine engine, the production version is set to switch to a commercial diesel, with a hybrid drive planned down the road.

Then there's that controller. The driver's station uses an off-the-shelf gaming controller instead of traditional tank controls, something the Army says shortens how long it takes to train a new driver, a real concern as fewer young people sign up to serve. The prototype also carries a remote weapon station and its own counter-drone radar, a clear nod to how much the battlefield has changed.

It's still early days. The Army plans a handful of these prototypes for troops to test, with serial production of the finished tank, to be designated the M1A3, targeted for around the end of the decade. The final version will look different again from this demonstrator. But the direction is set: the next Abrams will be lighter, smarter, more automated, and, at least from the driver's seat, it will feel a little like a video game.
